goals: Quantify the elevation gradient of peak snow water equivalent across the Wenatchee basin's 2683 m relief
Validate modeled peak SWE against 5 available SNOTEL stations
key_processes: Snow accumulation and melt driven by elevation-dependent temperature and precipitation

model_choice.rationale: ELM simulates snow accumulation/melt and outputs SWE by default. NLDAS-2 forcing at 0.125° provides elevation-resolved precipitation and temperature across the basin's 2683 m range, enabling representation of the elevation→climate→SWE mechanism.

answerable: Elevation control on peak SWE through NLDAS-2 spatially-varying forcing (temperature lapse, orographic precipitation)
Basin-wide SWE gradient across 2683 m elevation range

sampling_strategy.n_justification: 7 exploratory columns stratified across 4 elevation bands (1-2 per band, with 2 in the transition zone where SWE sensitivity is highest) resolve the univariate elevation gradient. Combined with 5 validation columns, total N=12 is sufficient for a single-driver question while keeping cost reasonable (~6 hours for 10-year runs).
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Exploratory columns placed at mid-slope positions within each elevation band to avoid extreme local topography (valley bottoms, ridgetops) where 12 km NLDAS forcing is least representative. Concentrate 2 columns in the rain-snow transition zone (800-1400 m) where peak SWE sensitivity to elevation is strongest. Validation columns pinned exactly to SNOTEL station coordinates.
sampling_strategy.replication: None — single column per exploratory stratum is sufficient for a gradient characterization; validation columns provide implicit replication within elevation bands where SNOTEL stations cluster.

sampling_plan.reason: Pinned to 5 SNOTEL station locations for co-located peak SWE validation
Samples <800 m rain-dominated zone to establish baseline minimal SWE
Samples 800-1100 m lower transition where rain begins shifting to snow
Samples 1100-1400 m upper transition where snow becomes dominant
Samples 1400-2000 m snow-dominated zone to capture peak SWE accumulation gradient
Samples >2000 m high-elevation zone to capture maximum SWE and late-season persistence

validation_design.comparison: co-located — model H2OSNO annual maximum at SNOTEL coordinates vs observed peak SWE
validation_design.metric: bias, RMSE, correlation across 5 stations and inter-annual variability

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: NLDAS-2 forcing (1980-2018 available, recommend 10-year period to capture inter-annual variability), native SSURGO soil at each location, default ELM snow parameterization

requires_capabilities.capability: SNOTEL station metadata (lat/lon/elevation) for the 5 Wenatchee basin stations
requires_capabilities.why: Needed to pin validation columns to exact station locations

requires_capabilities.capability: SNOTEL SWE time series ingest for the 5 stations
requires_capabilities.why: Needed to extract observed peak SWE for comparison to modeled H2OSNO annual maximum

requires_capabilities.capability: Peak SWE extraction from ELM H2OSNO output
requires_capabilities.why: Need to compute annual maximum SWE from daily/monthly H2OSNO time series for each column
requires_capabilities.blocks: Target variable calculation for validation and gradient analysis

assumptions: NLDAS-2 0.125° forcing adequately resolves the elevation gradient across the 2683 m range (verified in prior work showing ~15 distinct precip values across a similar-relief basin)
SNOTEL stations are distributed across the elevation gradient (not clustered in one band) — if all 5 are high-elevation, validation will not span the full gradient
10-year simulation period is sufficient to characterize inter-annual variability in peak SWE without requiring multi-decadal spin-up (snow is a fast state)
ELM's default snow parameterization is appropriate for Cascade snowpack (no calibration of snow albedo, density, or compaction parameters)
open_questions: What is the elevation distribution of the 5 SNOTEL stations — do they span the gradient or cluster high?
What simulation period should be used (recommend 2000-2010 or similar 10-year window with good SNOTEL data coverage)?
Should exploratory columns be placed to fill elevation gaps between SNOTEL stations, or independently stratified?
Is there interest in seasonal SWE dynamics (accumulation/melt timing) or only peak values?
